title: The Lean Startup
author: Eric Ries
theme: New ventures succeed by learning quickly what customers really want, using small experiments rather than detailed plans built on guesses.
summary: Eric Ries defines a startup as a group of people trying to create something new under conditions of extreme uncertainty. That definition covers a small team in a garage and a new unit inside a large company alike. Drawing on his own failures and successes, and on ideas from lean manufacturing at Toyota, he argues that traditional business planning breaks down in such conditions, because nobody yet knows who the customer is or what they will value.

The answer, he says, is to treat a venture as a series of experiments. Its real product in the early stages is validated learning: evidence, gathered from real customer behaviour, about which parts of the strategy work. Every plan rests on leap-of-faith assumptions, chiefly whether customers will find the product valuable and how the business will grow. These should be tested first.

The core tool is the Build-Measure-Learn loop. A team builds a minimum viable product, the smallest version that can test an assumption, measures how people actually respond, and learns whether to adjust. The aim is to move through this loop as fast as possible, so effort is not wasted on features nobody wants.

Ries warns against vanity metrics, such as total sign-ups, that rise and flatter the team without showing cause and effect. He proposes innovation accounting instead, using actionable measures like cohort analysis and split tests to judge whether changes truly improve results.

With that evidence, leaders face a regular decision: persevere with the current strategy or pivot, changing one element of it while keeping what has been learned. He also describes three engines of growth, driven by retention, word of mouth or paid acquisition, and recommends working in small batches.
Finally, he urges organisations to build learning into their routines, for example by asking why five times when problems occur, so that speed and quality improve together.
takeaway: Test your riskiest assumptions early with a minimum viable product, measure real behaviour, and decide honestly whether to persevere or pivot.

questions.q: How does Ries define a startup?
options: Any company less than five years old
A firm funded by venture capital
A human institution creating something new under extreme uncertainty
A technology company with fewer than fifty staff
questions.why: Ries ties the definition to uncertainty, not size or age, so it applies inside large companies too.

questions.q: What does Ries call the main measure of progress for an early-stage venture?
questions.why: Progress means gathering real evidence about what customers want, not simply building or selling more.

questions.q: What is a minimum viable product?
options: The cheapest product a firm can sell
A finished product released without marketing
A prototype shown only to investors
The smallest version of a product that lets a team test an assumption with real customers
questions.why: An MVP exists to start the learning loop with the least effort, not to be a polished release.

questions.q: Which sequence describes the core feedback loop in the book?
questions.why: Teams build something small, measure how customers respond, and learn what to change, aiming to cycle quickly.

questions.q: Why does Ries distrust vanity metrics such as total registered users?
options: They are too expensive to collect
Investors refuse to look at them
They can look impressive without showing whether a change caused any improvement
They are only useful for large companies
questions.why: Cumulative figures tend to rise anyway, hiding cause and effect, so they do not guide decisions.

questions.q: What does Ries mean by a pivot?
options: A structured change in one part of the strategy to test a new hypothesis
Raising a new round of funding
questions.why: A pivot keeps what has been learned while changing one element, such as the customer segment or the problem being solved.

questions.q: Which two leap-of-faith assumptions does Ries say should be tested first?
options: Whether customers will value the product and how the business will grow
questions.why: He calls these the value hypothesis and the growth hypothesis, the riskiest bets in any plan.

questions.q: What is innovation accounting designed to do?
options: Calculate the tax treatment of research spending
Track whether a venture is truly making progress using actionable metrics
Measure how many ideas employees submit
questions.why: It sets a baseline, tunes the product, and judges by real data whether to persevere or pivot.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three engines of growth Ries describes?
options: The viral engine, where existing customers bring in new ones
questions.why: He names sticky, viral and paid engines, each driven by a different source of customer growth.

questions.q: What practice does Ries borrow from Toyota to find the root cause of problems?
questions.why: Repeatedly asking why traces a problem to its human or process root so that a proportionate fix can be made.
